clue.text: See 6
Final defeat later adjusted in court

indicators.note: something adjusted has been altered, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged
the rearranged letters are placed inside the word for wooing

blocks.note: the word later, its letters rearranged
to court someone is to woo them

explanation.surface: A lawsuit that seemed won is lost on appeal when the judgment is later changed in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon's last battle gave the language a common phrase for a person's ultimate, decisive downfall.

clue.text: W.C. Fields's output?

blocks.note: surface reading: the films and gags produced by the American comedian W.C. Fields
setter's reading: W.C. is a water closet, so the comedy belongs to the lavatory field

explanation.walkthrough: W.C. Fields was a famous American film comic; read his initials as the lavatory abbreviation and his comic output becomes jokes about bodily functions.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude comedy about lavatories and bodily functions is what a comic from the water-closet field would naturally produce.

clue.text: Colour "Gone with the Wind", shot with extra energy

indicators.note: gone suggests the film title has been wrecked and its letters scattered into a new order
fabric shot with a thread has it woven through, so a letter is set inside the jumble

blocks.note: the words the and wind, their letters rearranged
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone instructs a colourist to tint the classic film, adding some extra energy to the shots.
explanation.walkthrough: Colour is a verb here, and the extra E goes between WHITE and ND.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something white is to give it a particular colour, so the past tense verb fits a verb used as an instruction-like definition.

clue.text: Slow moving thriller-writer?

definitions.note: read as a noun: one who moves slowly

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who strolls at a leisurely pace
second meaning: Eric ..., the English author of spy thrillers

explanation.surface: A sluggish suspense novelist whose plots fail to race along.
explanation.walkthrough: A thriller is supposed to move fast, which is the joke; the novelist is Eric Ambler, author of The Mask of Dimitrios.
explanation.definitionFit: One who ambles walks slowly and casually, and Eric Ambler was a celebrated British writer of espionage novels.

clue.text: Showing faith that could be hers, too, by following society's nepotism

indicators.note: following tells us the society abbreviation comes straight after the man of faith

blocks.note: Job, the biblical figure whose faith survived every trial
S is the standard abbreviation for society
a playful hint: the favours are labelled as going to men, though women could get them as well

explanation.surface: A woman shows her loyalty, hoping that cronyism will reward her as much as any man.
explanation.walkthrough: The last third is a cryptic nudge rather than strict wordplay: the phrase names the men who get the posts, while the clue notes women could benefit too.
explanation.definitionFit: Handing posts to friends and allies rather than the best candidates is the classic idiom for favouritism and cronyism.

clue.text: Be unfaithful to wife No. 3 and what she may then turn!

blocks.note: surface reading: a husband straying from his third marriage
setter's reading: once betrayed, the wife may turn on her husband, echoing the second word of the phrase

explanation.surface: A thrice-married man strays, and his latest wife may well round on him.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the plain opening; the exclamation suggests the wronged wife will turn on him, supplying the little word that closes the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To betray a partner by having an affair is the everyday phrasal-verb meaning of the answer.

clue.text: Lock cleaner so engrosses overacting Teletubby

indicators.note: to engross is to absorb wholly, so one word swallows the others inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
a ham is an actor who overacts
Po is the smallest, red Teletubby

explanation.surface: A security device gets polished while a hammy children's TV character holds the audience rapt.
explanation.walkthrough: Lock means a strand of hair, not a door fastening; the Teletubbies are characters from a British children's television show.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair is made of locks, and the product used to wash it is the obvious cleaner for them.

clue.text: Casually sauntered around Abraham''s home and took the loot with no value?

definitions.text: took the loot with no value?

indicators.note: doing something casually means in a loose, haphazard way, so the letters fall out of order
around says the jumbled letters wrap about the patriarch's city

blocks.note: the word sauntered, its letters rearranged
Ur of the Chaldees, Abraham's birthplace in Genesis

explanation.surface: A thief strolled round the patriarch's house and made off with goods that turned out worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on two senses: stripped of treasure after the loot is taken, and not valued at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not prized or held dear is unvalued, and the clue jokes that losing the treasure leaves it this way.

clue.text: Go down while on-line

blocks.note: surface reading: a computer or website crashing while connected to the internet
setter's reading: hanging on a rope, so descending a cliff with one

explanation.walkthrough: On-line suggests the internet, but the line is a climbing rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Climbers descend a rock face by sliding down a doubled rope, which is exactly going down while on a line.

clue.text: Broke off key?

blocks.note: first meaning: without any banknotes, penniless
second meaning: without musical notes, so no tune at all

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second sense: music without notes cannot be in any key.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no banknotes means being out of money, while having no musical notes leaves nothing tuneful to sing.

clue.text: Contribution to a paltry allowance?

indicators.note: a contribution is a part of the whole, so the answer is a part of the words that follow

blocks.note: the tail of the first word joined to the head of the second

explanation.surface: Someone chips a small coin into a meagre pocket-money fund.
explanation.walkthrough: A ryal (or rial) is an old English gold coin, so the whole clue also describes one being added to a meagre sum.
explanation.definitionFit: An antique coin of the realm is just the kind of small sum someone might add to a meagre allowance.

clue.text: King 22''s convenience ...

blocks.note: surface reading: the private lavatory of King John, as 22 is the word for a lavatory
setter's reading: a royal room, the chamber where a monarch sits in state

explanation.walkthrough: A convenience is a public toilet and a john is a lavatory, while a throne is slang for one too; so the king's state chamber doubles as his loo.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's ceremonial chamber holds the royal seat, and that seat is also jokey slang for a lavatory.

clue.text: ... would be above this par ...

blocks.note: surface reading: the royal room would rise above an ordinary level
setter's reading: a royal lavatory is better than the merely basic level, which is named after a lavatory too

explanation.walkthrough: Continues from the previous clue; bog is British slang for toilet, so a king's lavatory sits above the ordinary lavatory grade.
explanation.definitionFit: Par is the normal or average level, and the British idiom for something entirely ordinary and unremarkable names that level.

clue.text: A game like this, initially for consumption of everybody

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the next word counts

blocks.note: so can mean in this way
the opening letter of the word
consumption is the old name for tuberculosis, abbreviated TB
all means every person

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a sport like this one so that everyone can enjoy watching it.
explanation.walkthrough: Consumption looks like eating or viewing, but it is the old word for the lung disease.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a team sport closely related to baseball, played with a larger ball, so it is one kind of game.

clue.text: Cronin''s remains described by epitaph in princely Indian state

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw around it, so the tombstone inscription surrounds the other pieces

blocks.note: the novelist A.J. Cronin, by his initials
ash is what remains after cremation
rest in peace, the stock gravestone inscription

explanation.surface: A novelist's ashes lie under an inscription in some grand region of the subcontinent.
explanation.walkthrough: State is not a territory but a condition: the status of being a raja.
explanation.definitionFit: A raja is an Indian prince, and the suffix denoting office or condition turns that title into the princely status itself.

clue.text: Lose it, ie the clue to "departmental"

blocks.note: the first part of the word, depart, means leave
the second part, mental, is slang for crazy, which a British idiom also expresses

explanation.surface: An exasperated solver snaps while explaining how a puzzle hints at a word about office departments.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer, read in two parts, would itself be a cryptic clue for departmental, since go means depart and the rest means mental.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose it is to lose one's sanity or temper, and the British idiom means exactly to go mad.

clue.text: See 17
... with suitable embarrassment on the cards?

definitions.note: a noun phrase: a blush fit for a king
a phrase pointing to something held in a card game

blocks.note: first meaning: a red face fit for a monarch, a regal blush
second meaning: the top poker hand, ace to ten all in one suit

explanation.walkthrough: Continues the King John story; suitable recalls a suit of cards, and a flush is also what a toilet does.
explanation.definitionFit: A flush is a reddening of the face, fitting for royalty, and the unbeatable poker hand carries the same two-word name.

clue.text: We are nearly always going about, tired of old people

indicators.note: nearly means not quite complete, so the final letter of the phrase is dropped
going about means travelling around something, so one word encircles the other

blocks.note: ay (or aye) is an old word for always, as in for ay
taken as written, the two words run together
surface padding: the folk who used the archaic word

explanation.surface: A weary group complain that they are almost always on the move and are sick of the elderly.
explanation.walkthrough: Of old marks the word as archaic, and people rounds off the surface as those who used it.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an archaic and poetic form meaning weary, as in Shakespeare's line about growing weary of the sun.

clue.text: See 3
3 writer of "Biggle"?

definitions.note: cross-reference to the first word of the 3-down answer

blocks.note: Captain W.E. Johns wrote the Biggles books; one Biggle needs one less letter

explanation.surface: A question about who wrote a single adventure of the famous fictional pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: Biggles, the flying ace, was created by W.E. Johns; dropping the plural ending from the books drops the same letter from the author.
explanation.definitionFit: John is everyday slang, mostly American, for a lavatory, which is the first word of the 3-down answer.

clue.text: Worker's so long coming back in one, he's admitted

indicators.note: coming back means returning, so the farewell is read from its end
in places the returned farewell inside the number word
admitted means let inside, so the combination goes within the pronoun

blocks.note: the pronoun taken as written
taken as written
so long is a casual farewell, like bye

explanation.surface: A labourer's long absence ends as he returns and is let in by someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Worker is the term for the sterile female insect in a hive; the farewell sits in the number, and that sits in the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Most members of a hive are female workers that forage for nectar and tend the colony, so the insect is the archetypal worker.

clue.text: Racing certainty from Spooner bankrupted the writer

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the start sounds trade places

blocks.note: bust means bankrupted, its opening sound swapped
the writer is the setter, so me, its opening sound swapped

explanation.surface: A gambler blames a sure-fire tip on the horses for ruining him.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer means the setter, i.e. me.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has to happen is a dead cert, and the hyphenated noun is used for a sure winner or certainty.

clue.text: Winning repeatedly in lists?

definitions.note: read as entered on a register

blocks.note: first meaning: enjoying a run of successes
second meaning: entered ..., a register of names

explanation.walkthrough: Lists suggests the jousting lists where knights win bouts, but here it means registers.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll is an official list of names, and the idiom for a winning streak is also being entered on such a list.

clue.text: Queen's University journal backing a climber

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the two abbreviations are read in reverse order

blocks.note: U is the standard abbreviation for university
J is an abbreviation for journal
a liana is a woody climbing vine of tropical forests

explanation.surface: A university paper supports a mountaineer, appearing to report on a royal academic institution.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen's University suggests the Belfast institution, but Queen is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Juliana reigned as Queen of the Netherlands from 1948 to 1980, so her name defines a queen by example.
